question: I'm writing a related-work section on The AI Scientist (Lu et al.). Which later papers actually extend its method, as opposed to just citing it in passing?
graph_reason: By far the widest and most checkable coverage — it separates extension from background with named quoted relationships (AIGS's "the coding language adopted in previous work (Lu et al., 2024)", CoI's novelty-check reuse) and an accurate roll-call of the benchmark/peer-review/risk citing set (MLGym, ScienceAgentBench, RE-Bench, MLRC-Bench, Jr. AI Scientist, "The More You Automate…", AgentRxiv-builds-on-Agent-Laboratory), though the Kosmos "≈8× more discovery cycles" figure and the Nature 2026 follow-up are the shakiest items, and it misses Dolphin, the clearest third-party extension.
web_reason: The only answer to surface Dolphin (Yuan et al., Shanghai AI Lab), which is genuinely the paper that names AI Scientist's no-feedback-to-ideation gap and closes that loop, and the only one to note v2's own admission that it does not always beat v1 when a good template exists — but its AI-Researcher mechanism description ("bidirectional mappings between mathematical formulations and code", mentor/student refinement) and the NeurIPS 2025 venue attribution are stated more confidently than I can support, and its overall coverage is much thinner than A's.
null_reason: Correct on everything it commits to (v2's template→tree-search replacement, CycleResearcher's RL-against-an-automated-reviewer loop, CoI-Agent's idea-generation focus, Agent Laboratory / co-scientist / Robin as convergent-not-derived) and admirably explicit about which items to verify before citing, but it covers the smallest slice of the citing literature and its "extends a stage" grouping is loosely argued — CycleResearcher is arguably an independent training paradigm rather than an extension of Lu et al.'s pipeline.
fabrication_notes: No clear fabrications in any answer; all named systems (AI Scientist-v2, Dolphin, AI-Researcher, AIGS/Baby-AIGS, CoI-Agent, CycleResearcher, Curie, Agent Laboratory, Kosmos, Robin, AgentRxiv, Jr. AI Scientist, and A's benchmark list) exist. question: Is the field actually agreed that LLMs can come up with genuinely novel research ideas, or do the studies disagree?
graph_reason: Maps the disagreement at two levels — capability (Si et al. vs MLGym vs the Gupta/Pruthi plagiarism audit) and, more valuably, measurement validity (MLRC-Bench, SCI-IDEA vs MLR-Judge/ResearchAgent/Gu-Krenn, NovBench) — with named, overwhelmingly real papers and checkable pairwise relations; minor risk sits in unverifiable specifics (SCI-IDEA's 3–4 point gap and r=0.02–0.17, "NovBench", the 2026 astronomy study) and it oddly omits the single most direct rebuttal, the same authors' Ideation-Execution Gap.
web_reason: Correctly identifies the sharpest structure in this debate — the same group's own Ideation-Execution Gap (43 executors, 100+ hours, LLM ideas dropping more on every metric) rebutting their ICLR 2025 result — plus Beel et al.'s independent Sakana audit with accurate details (micro-batching misjudged as novel, ~42% experiment failure), and it scopes its own limits honestly to NLP/ML; narrower coverage than A and it misses the evaluation-validity literature entirely.
null_reason: Accurate on Si/Yang/Hashimoto (novelty edge, feasibility trade-off, diversity collapse, self-eval unreliability) and honest in flagging that it could not name the execution follow-up — which is exactly the right behaviour — but it rests on only two named papers, substitutes community controversy over The AI Scientist for actual counter-evidence, and so gives the researcher little to chase.
fabrication_notes: None confidently fabricated. Watch-items in A: the exact SCI-IDEA numbers (3–4 point LLM-judge inflation, r=0.02–0.17), "NovBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Academic Paper Novelty Assessment" (plausible but I cannot confirm the title; related work such as SchNovel/NoveltyBench exists and could be conflated), and the "2026 astronomy" study's date/title. B's unnamed execution follow-up is real (Si, Yang, Hashimoto, "The Ideation-Execution Gap", 2025) and B was right to flag rather than guess it. C's three papers all check out, including Beel et al.'s Sakana evaluation.
